analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to approve every major federal regulation before it can take effect.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; after being introduced in September 2010 with 13 Republican sponsors, it sat in the Senate Homeland Security Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, a major federal regulation takes effect automatically unless Congress passes a law to stop it. This bill would flip that: any rule the government estimates would affect the economy by $100 million or more could not take effect unless both the House and Senate pass, and the President signs, a resolution approving it within 90 days. If Congress simply did nothing, the rule would die. The President could temporarily activate a rule for 90 days in a health or safety emergency, for criminal enforcement, or for national security.
analysis.who_benefits: Large regulated businesses — in energy, manufacturing, finance, and other sectors — would gain an effective veto over major rules. They would only need to persuade one chamber of Congress to sit on a resolution of approval, and the rule disappears without a vote.

how_it_helps.text: Reverses the default for major rules: instead of taking effect unless Congress disapproves them, rules with an estimated $100 million or more annual economic effect would have no force unless Congress affirmatively approves them [S2][S3].
If no approval resolution is enacted within 90 days of introduction, the rule is deemed not approved and cannot take effect, meaning inaction by either chamber kills it [S2][S3].
The bill's stated purpose is to make Congress, rather than unelected agency staff, accountable for costly rules, citing 80 major rules issued in 2009 alone [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost through rules that are delayed or die silently: protections for air and water quality, workplace safety, consumer finance, food safety, and drug approval all come through major rules that would now require an affirmative act of Congress to exist.

drawbacks.text: The Constitution gives Congress the legislative power, and agencies today write binding rules with billion-dollar effects without any member of Congress ever voting on them; the bill argues rule drafters are not directly accountable to voters [S3].
The mechanism rewards inaction: any industry lobby that can stop one chamber from voting on an approval resolution kills a rule outright, without the public ever seeing a recorded vote on it [S3].

The emergency exception is narrow and time-limited — a 90-day window for imminent health or safety threats, criminal enforcement, or national security — and it expires unless Congress affirmatively approves the rule [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument is genuine: Congress delegates lawmaking to agencies and then avoids ownership of the results. But this design solves that by making it maximally easy to block any major rule — one committee chair or one chamber's inaction kills a $100 million rule without a vote or a record. It would shift power from expert agencies to whichever concentrated interest can best freeze Congress, and the public would absorb the loss in weaker protections rather than seeing the trade-off debated openly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim DeMint and 12 other Republican senators introduced the bill on September 22, 2010 [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs — its only action in the Congress [S5].
No further action, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died without a vote, the existing regulatory system stayed intact: agencies kept the ability to issue major rules without congressional approval, and the public kept rules on health, safety, and finance that would otherwise have needed a new act of Congress to survive. Regulated industries gained nothing this time, though the same proposal was reintroduced in later Congresses.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors were Republicans, and the bill went nowhere in the Democratic-controlled Senate, which took no action beyond the initial referral [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Regulated industries (energy, manufacturing, finance, and other businesses subject to federal rules)
industries.note: The bill would give any major rule's opponents a way to kill it by keeping a congressional vote from ever happening, so businesses facing $100 million compliance costs would gain a powerful delay-and-die tool. The public pays in rules on pollution, workplace safety, and consumer protection that die without a debate.

Agencies would lose the ability to put major rules into effect on their own authority, needing an act of Congress for each one. For ordinary people this is the mechanism that would slow or kill health, safety, and financial rules.
